evals.prompt: Define the Next.js request-preprocessing layer in 2-3 sentences. Name the current file/function convention, where it runs in the request lifecycle, and the four response shapes it can return.
expected_elements: A single async function in one root file that runs before route resolution for requests matching its matcher config
As of Next.js 16 the file is proxy.ts (function proxy, Node.js runtime); middleware.ts (function middleware, Edge by default) is deprecated but retained for Edge use cases
It receives a NextRequest and returns a NextResponse in one of four shapes: next (pass through), rewrite, redirect, or a direct response
It runs once per request before any page render, Server Component fetch, Server Action, or Route Handler

evals.prompt: Explain why the runtime (Node.js for proxy.ts vs Edge for middleware.ts) is the load-bearing axis of this layer. What does each runtime allow, and what discipline persists regardless of runtime?
expected_elements: proxy.ts runs on Node.js only (its runtime config throws if set) — full Node APIs (crypto, fs, Buffer) are available

middleware.ts runs on Edge by default (Node.js opt-in since 15.5) — Web Crypto/fetch/Web Streams only, no Node crypto/fs/child_process, plus a per-plan gzip bundle ceiling where one Node-only import breaks the build
The runtime turned 'no DB query' from a capability wall into a performance/architecture rule — on Node it is possible but still forbidden because the cost multiplies across every matched request
Regardless of runtime: keep it small and fast (target <10ms p99); no per-request I/O

evals.prompt: What is the architectural trade this layer makes, and why does Vercel now recommend reaching for native features (next.config redirects/headers, the WAF, route-level auth) before writing proxy code?
expected_elements: The trade is breadth for power: it can shape the whole request/response edge in one place but runs on every matched request, has no per-route knowledge until rewrite/redirect resolves, and cannot read the response body
next.config redirects/headers run before proxy in the routing chain and cost no per-request execution — push static decisions there
Use proxy only when the decision is dynamic (depends on a cookie, header, geo, or A/B bucket) or a per-request value (CSP nonce) is genuinely needed
A smaller, faster proxy is a better proxy; the Next.js 16 rename discourages Express-style 'do everything here' misuse

evals.prompt: A team wants to redirect logged-out users away from /dashboard and /admin to /login. Walk through how to implement this correctly with proxy, and state explicitly what this implementation does and does not guarantee.
expected_elements: Check the session cookie's presence (request.cookies.get) and NextResponse.redirect to /login when missing on protected paths, scoped via a matcher to /dashboard/:path* and /admin/:path*
This is a UX optimization only — the cookie is checked for presence, not cryptographically verified; no per-request DB lookup belongs here
Authorization MUST still be enforced at the route, Route Handler, Server Action, and Data Access Layer — the proxy gate can be bypassed (CVE-2025-29927) or silently skipped by a matcher exclusion
Every Server Action must verify authz itself because a matcher exclusion skips Server Function calls on that path

evals.prompt: Geo-routing broke after upgrading to Next.js 15 because request.geo is undefined. How should the agent read country/IP now, and what caveats apply on and off Vercel?
expected_elements: request.geo and request.ip were removed from NextRequest in Next.js 15
On Vercel, read via geolocation(request) and ipAddress(request) from @vercel/functions (install the package; the Next.js 15 codemod does this)
Off Vercel, parse the platform's geo headers (e.g. x-vercel-ip-country or the CDN equivalent) and read defensively — values may be undefined locally or wrong behind another proxy
Geo is not a security boundary; for hard enforcement prefer the platform firewall/WAF

evals.prompt: Distinguish middleware-patterns from route-handler-design, server-actions-design, and security-fundamentals. Give a mechanism-level reason each differs, not just the label.
expected_elements: route-handler-design runs AFTER route resolution for one route and one method; the proxy layer runs ONCE BEFORE route resolution across many routes via a matcher — they compose, proxy passes through to the handler
server-actions-design owns the in-app mutation surface; a Server Action passes through proxy but a matcher exclusion silently skips it, so authz must live inside each action, not only in proxy

security-fundamentals owns the CSP policy, hardening, and the actual authorization architecture; proxy is one delivery surface for headers and a UX optimization for auth redirects — never the policy or the security boundary
Names the differing mechanism (before vs after route resolution, delivery surface vs policy owner), not just the skill name

evals.prompt: Correct this statement: 'Next.js middleware is where I enforce auth — if the matcher protects /admin and I check the session cookie there, /admin is secure.'
expected_elements: This layer is NOT a security boundary — CVE-2025-29927 let attackers bypass it entirely by spoofing x-middleware-subrequest, skipping every auth check
The matcher is not a security perimeter: May-2026 bypasses reached protected pages through transport variants (.rsc/segment-prefetch, dynamic-route injection) the matcher never enumerated
Real authorization belongs at the route, Server Action, and Data Access Layer; the proxy auth check is only a fast UX redirect
Stay patched (>=14.2.25/>=15.2.3 for 29927; >=15.5.18/>=16.2.6 for the May-2026 cluster, one patch higher on Turbopack) and enforce authz at the route regardless

evals.prompt: What would you check to verify a proxy/middleware implementation is correct and safe?
expected_elements: A matcher is set with build-time constants excluding _next/static, _next/image, favicon.ico, metadata files, and typically webhooks; matcher coverage is tested (including a transport/data variant) with next/experimental/testing/server

Authorization is enforced at the route/handler/action/DAL — not only in proxy — and a defense-in-depth test bypasses proxy and asserts an unauthorized caller is still rejected; framework patched against CVE-2025-29927 and the May-2026 cluster

No per-request DB queries or I/O adding >10ms even on Node; geo/IP read via @vercel/functions; cookies read via request.cookies and written via response.cookies.set (no cookies() import); modified request headers use NextResponse.next({ request: { headers } })

rewrite vs redirect vs direct response is chosen by whether the URL should visibly change; per-request CSP nonces are generated server-side, never cached/shared/derived from inbound headers, and their dynamic-rendering cost is accepted
